title: Generic Max Function
story: You've written `max_int(3, 7)` and `max_float(2.5, 4.1)`. Now you need `max_str("apple", "zebra")`. The logic is the same: compare two values and return the larger one. Can generics help here?
why: Generic functions with comparison operations demonstrate how generics interact with type-specific behavior — the function is generic, but the comparison works because XIOM supports it for basic types.
analogy: A generic max function is like a measuring tape. Whether you're measuring height (Int), length (Float64), or alphabetical order (Str), the same tool works. The measuring tape doesn't care what it's measuring — it just compares which is bigger. The `[T]` is the tape saying 'I work on anything you can line up and compare.'
try_it: Write `my_equals[T](a: T, b: T) -> Bool` that returns true if the two values are equal. Try it with Int, Str, and Bool. Write a `clamp[T](value: T, min: T, max: T) -> T` function that returns `min` if value < min, `max` if value > max, and `value` otherwise. Test it with different types.
tips: The `>` operator works on any T that supports comparison — Int, Float64, Str, and Char all do
Both parameters must be the SAME type T — you can't mix `my_max(5, 3.14)` because Int and Float64 are different
The return type matches the parameter type — max of two Ints returns Int, max of two Strs returns Str
common_mistakes: Mixing types in a generic call: `my_max(5, 3.14)` fails because 5 is Int and 3.14 is Float64 — convert one first
Assuming `>` works on custom structs — it doesn't unless the struct derives a comparison trait
Putting the comparison logic OUTSIDE the generic function and expecting it to work — the comparison must be inside the generic body
